newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan opposition defends CEPA power deal.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan opposition defends CEPA power deal.

text.p: Pakistani opposition leader Benazir Bhutto threatened on Wednesday to go to court to defend a power project of Hong Kong-based Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd (CEPA) against a government move to terminate the deal.
The former prime minister told the National Assembly (lower house) that the government's move to cancel the project in her home province of Sindh was discriminatory.
"We will strongly protest,...this is criminal," she said. "We will consult our legal experts to go to the Supreme Court to see if it was discrimination against a smaller province."
Water and Power Minister Nisar Ali Khan told the National Assembly on Tuesday that Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government had decided to terminate the deal with CEPA by "mutual agreement".

But a CEPA official in Islamabad said the government had not conveyed its decision to his company, in which U.S. power giant Southern Co has an 80 percent stake and Hong Kong's Hopewell Holdings Ltd 20 percent.
"We have absolutely no official information or intimation of termination of the contract," CEPA resident director Latif Chaudhry told Reuters by telephone.
"As far as we are concerned, we are working as usual, all our staff here, in Karachi and in Hong Kong are working as they have always been working," Chaudhry said.

Khan acknowledged that CEPA had not yet been informed. "It's a question of intent," he told Reuters on Wednesday as he referred to his Tuesday's speech, in which he also said Pakistan would be unable to buy electricity from CEPA at the rate negotiated by the previous government of Bhutto.

Earlier this month, a Pakistan government official had said that the Economic Coordination Committee of the cabinet had decided to re-negotiate the deal with CEPA, which was struck in June 1995 when Islamabad issued a Letter of Support, enabling the company to complete other formalities.
Under the agreement, CEPA was to build eight 660-megwatt, coal-based, thermal power plants at Keti Bundar, about 60 km (37 miles) west of the port city of Karachi, for a total cost of $5.5 billion.
CEPA also had plans to develop a 14-metre-deep sea port in Sindh and also set up a special industrial zone at the site with a total cost of $1.0 billion.
The port was to be developed in three years and ships with a cargo handling capacity of 70,000 tonnes could berth at 14 planned jetties.
